purpose.intro: The module ships the engine (`shared/auth-config/`: types, resolver, validation); the product ships the config instance (`configs/user-organization-mgmt/auth/`). Add a rule to the config and every consumer — registration flow, login form, the gate — picks it up with no code change.

claims.text: **orgAction** — how a membership is being established: `create | join` (absent for login, recovery, and the gate)
They are separate axes because a flat intent list made contradictory combinations expressible (registration+authentication) and couldn't say "register AND create a company".

reference.statement: Any auth moment is described by two single-valued axes:

claims.text: **A clause naming a field the context lacks does NOT match.** The gate evaluates membership contexts with no `intent` — so a clause that includes `intent` can never fire at the gate.

**Extra context fields don't prevent matching** (subset check). A clause `{ membershipOrgType: "company" }` fires both during a company-targeted registration (whose context also carries `intent`) and at the standing gate.

snippets.code:
when: [clauseA, clauseB]   // clauseA OR clauseB   (any-of)
{ intent: "registration", membershipOrgType: "company" }  // AND within a clause
{ intent: ["registration", "authentication"] }            // any-of within a key
notWhen: [clauseC]         // ...AND NOT clauseC (veto, same clause semantics)

reference.statement: A clause matches when EVERY key it names is present in the context with an allowed value. Two consequences that bite:

claims.text: **Intent-keyed clauses** enforce during their flow only.
**Membership-keyed clauses** stand forever: they fire during org-targeted flows AND at the gate for existing members.
An obligation that must hold for members must be authored membership-keyed. Example of the classic bug (this exact shape shipped in a draft):
Why it matters: rules added to the config after users exist must catch those users at the gate. Intent-keyed rules silently don't.

reference.statement: Identifiers are a map `identifier → policy`, not a list of grant rules. In a union-of-grants list, a `notWhen` on one rule can't claw back what another rule granted — restrictions don't compose. As a unique key, each identifier's visibility is decided in exactly one place.

`resolveIdentifiers(config, ctx)` → visible identifier names. `resolveFactors(config, ctx)` → factor specs (serialize with `factorKey`: `password`, `otp:phone`, `link:email`, `totp`). `resolveRequirements(config, ctx)` → bare requirement names. `resolveObligations(config, ctx)` → typed obligations with the specifics a screen needs (`identityTypes[]` — any listed type satisfies — / `factorMethod` / `dataField` / `consent[]`).

`validateAuthConfig` runs on config import (fails boot): factors offered at authentication must be auth-capable, membership-required factors must be gate-capable, OTP needs an OTP-capable `deliveredVia`, `deviceOtp` is rejected (catalogued vocabulary without runtime support), every registrable identifier must be code-deliverable or delegated (oidc) — an identity is born by code proof or OIDC callback; anything else has no way to be born — and a password factor must carry `config.minLength >= 8`, the provider's hard floor (the DSL is the one authority on password acceptability; the provider's own checks are pinned off in kratos.yml). `validateOrgLifecycle` checks the org lifecycle entries (owner role present for user-creatable types, no duplicates) — config that stays ready for the org stage.
